  • Compression — apply a bandage firmly (not too tight) to reduce swelling and bleeding.
  • Elevation — raise the injured area (e.g. place a pillow under the ankle) to reduce bleeding and swelling via gravity.
  • Referral — refer to a qualified professional (doctor/physiotherapist) for diagnosis and treatment.

Caution: While ice reduces inflammation in the early stages, prolonged use can reduce blood flow and cause nerve damage — ice should never be applied continuously or directly to skin.

bandDescriptors.full: 5/5 — Correctly defines all five RICER steps (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, Referral) with an accurate explanation of what each achieves. Includes a specific caution about ice — e.g. do not apply directly to skin or continuously; prolonged use can cause nerve damage.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/5 — Defines most RICER steps correctly but misses one step or the explanation of one step is inaccurate. The ice caution may be absent or vague.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/5 — Names some RICER letters without adequate explanation. May only list the acronym with no detail about what each step does.

writtenQuestions.q: Outline the management of hard tissue injuries, distinguishing between the management of fractures and dislocations. (6 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Fracture management requires: using DRSABCD, controlling bleeding, treating shock, using a splint and bandage to immobilise the area, and seeking immediate medical assistance. Medical attention is required when there is obvious deformity, uncontrolled bleeding, or the casualty cannot complete TOTAPS. Simple (closed) fractures keep bone beneath skin; compound (open) fractures involve bone protruding through skin and are more serious.

Dislocation management requires: never attempting to relocate the displaced bone (this risks further damage), securing the joint with a splint for full immobilisation, applying ice and elevation, using a supportive bandage, and seeking immediate medical attention. A subluxation — where the bone briefly pops out and returns — also requires rehabilitation and possibly surgery.

bandDescriptors.full: 5–6/6 — Describes management of BOTH fractures (DRSABCD, splint and bandage to immobilise, control bleeding, seek medical assistance) AND dislocations (never attempt to relocate, splint, ice, elevation, immediate medical attention). Distinguishes simple from compound fractures and/or mentions subluxation.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/6 — Describes both fracture and dislocation management but with incomplete detail on one. May omit the critical 'never relocate' rule for dislocations, or not distinguish fracture types.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/6 — Describes only one type of hard tissue injury, or provides only a general management approach without distinguishing fractures from dislocations.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain progressive mobilisation and the rules that must be followed when applying it after injury. (4 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Progressive mobilisation is the gradual reintroduction of movement to an injured area after RICER has been applied and the acute inflammatory phase has passed. It involves gradually extending the range of movement through light stretches and rotations to reduce scar tissue build-up and restore mobility.

Mobilisation can be active (performed by the athlete) or passive (the injured part is manipulated by another person). Rules that must be followed include: (1) confirm no fracture is present — an X-ray may be needed; (2) do not begin during the acute inflammatory phase; (3) movements must be slow and progressive, not sharp or rapid; and (4) movements must remain within a pain-free range at all times.

bandDescriptors.full: 4/4 — Defines progressive mobilisation (gradual reintroduction of movement after the acute phase), mentions both active and passive forms, and states at least two rules: no fracture present, not during the acute inflammatory phase, movements slow and progressive, within a pain-free range at all times.
bandDescriptors.partial: 2–3/4 — Defines progressive mobilisation correctly but only states one rule, the active/passive distinction is missing, or the timing (after RICER/acute phase) is not mentioned.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1/4 — Vague description of 'moving the injury carefully' without defining progressive mobilisation or listing the rules that apply.

writtenQuestions.q: Describe how graduated exercise, including stretching and conditioning, is used in rehabilitation. (6 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Graduated exercise encompasses stretching and conditioning to rebuild fitness after injury.

Stretching: Stretching the injured area ensures healing without scarring. Scarring shortens muscle, making it prone to re-injury. The most appropriate methods are static stretching and PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) stretching, which reduce muscle tension, increase circulation and restore range of motion. Movements initially stay within pain barriers and gradually increase as strength improves.

Conditioning: Uses the overload principle to progressively increase physical stress and build adaptation. The program targets cardiorespiratory fitness plus strength, power and local muscular endurance around the injured area (specificity). It is designed to prevent muscle atrophy. As strength returns, further resistance is applied and weight-bearing exercises are introduced if the area can support them.

bandDescriptors.full: 5–6/6 — Explains BOTH stretching (static and PNF methods, prevents scarring, restores range of motion) AND conditioning (overload principle, specificity, prevents muscle atrophy, progressive resistance). Describes how each component is applied in rehabilitation.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/6 — Addresses both stretching and conditioning but with incomplete detail on one. May name PNF without explaining it, or describe overload without linking to specificity or atrophy prevention.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/6 — Describes only one component (stretching or conditioning) or provides only a general statement about 'exercise during rehab' without explaining the principles or methods involved.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain the use of heat and cold therapy in rehabilitation, including when each should and should not be used. (5 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Cold therapy is used for the immediate treatment of injury as it prevents swelling by constricting blood vessels and limiting internal bleeding. It is also useful after exercise during rehabilitation when the injured area has been through a workout. Methods include ice packs, ice massage, cold water immersion and topical cold spray. Caution: prolonged cold use reduces blood flow and can cause nerve damage.

Heat therapy should not be used in the early (acute) stage while bleeding is still occurring, as it promotes blood flow and would worsen swelling. Heat is used in later rehabilitation for chronic injuries to promote circulation, relax muscles, decrease muscle spasm and tightness, and reduce pain. Methods include heat packs, hydrotherapy, infra-red lamps, ultrasound and shortwave machines.

bandDescriptors.full: 5/5 — Accurately describes BOTH cold therapy (immediate/acute phase, constricts blood vessels, prevents swelling; caution: prolonged use causes nerve damage) AND heat therapy (later rehabilitation/chronic phase, promotes blood flow, relaxes muscles; not in acute phase while bleeding is occurring). Names at least one method for each.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/5 — Describes both therapies but the timing distinction (cold = acute/immediate, heat = later/chronic) is incomplete. May fail to include a caution for one therapy.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/5 — Describes only one therapy, or confuses when each should be used. No cautions provided.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain how total body fitness is maintained and restored during a rehabilitation program. (5 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Total body fitness in rehabilitation means regaining full pre-injury fitness by targeting all muscle groups and energy systems — not just the injured area. The program must apply all principles of training, particularly progressive overload.

Activities used to promote total body fitness include treadmill work, rowing or cycling ergometers, swimming and water-resistance activities, weight training, and walking/light jogging. Adaptations to aim for include: strengthening of ligaments and tendons, complete absence of pain, and full confidence in the injured area.

Flexibility, strength and endurance are maintained through activities specific to the sport that do not endanger recovery. The program is complete when the athlete can participate in all elements of a full training session — warm-up, skills, drills, match play and cool-down — without pain.

bandDescriptors.full: 5/5 — Explains that total body fitness targets all muscle groups and energy systems (not just the injury). Describes at least two appropriate activities (e.g. treadmill, swimming, cycling, weight training). Links to the progressive overload principle. States the program is complete when the athlete can participate pain-free in all elements of a full training session.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/5 — Addresses total body fitness and mentions activities, but the overload/progressive principle is absent or the completion criteria is not stated clearly.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/5 — Vague description of 'keeping fit during rehab' without addressing all muscle groups, specific activities, or training principles.

writtenQuestions.q: Outline how the indicators of readiness to return to play are used following an ankle sprain. (3 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
After an ankle sprain the athlete must demonstrate all five indicators before return:

  • Elasticity — the new tissue has been stretched to promote flexibility
  • Strength — equal to the uninjured side (tested via single-leg hop)
  • Mobility — full agility and direction changes without pain
  • Pain-free — during both light and strenuous exercise
  • Balance — able to balance on the injured limb alone

These are confirmed through sport-specific skill tests. Only when all criteria are met can the athlete return to competition.

bandDescriptors.full: 3/3 — Names all five indicators of readiness (Elasticity, Strength, Mobility, Pain-free, Balance) with a brief explanation of each. States that ALL five must be met before return and applies them to an ankle sprain context.
bandDescriptors.partial: 2/3 — Names at least three indicators correctly with some explanation, but not all five are listed or applied to the ankle sprain context.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1/3 — Names one or two indicators only, or provides only a vague description of 'the athlete must be healthy' without listing specific criteria.

writtenQuestions.q: How are skill and physical tests used to indicate an athlete's readiness to return to play after injury? (8 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Return to play is a coordinated effort between the athlete and medical staff. All athletes returning to play should undertake and pass comprehensive skill and physical related tests. These tests should include a demonstration of pain-free full range of motion. For example, an athlete who injures their shoulder in football should be able to complete a circumduction test free of any musculoskeletal pain. Any discomfort or pain indicates the athlete is not ready to return.

In addition to being pain-free, the athlete must have a normal degree of mobility at the injury site. For example, a soccer player with a torn ligament should undergo physical skills such as agility and mobility tests (e.g. Illinois Agility Test) to ensure they can successfully bear full weight and complete all pre-injury duties.

Strength and flexibility testing involves comparison between the injured and uninjured limb. This ensures the athlete has recovered full mobility and strength to prevent recurrence or a secondary injury, and ensures optimal performance upon return. The athlete must perform exercises related to their sport — e.g. kicking a football with both legs. If the athlete demonstrates 90–95% of strength and range of motion returned to the injured limb, they are determined fit to play.

Generic skill tests can also compare an athlete pre-injury to post-injury — for example, using the vertical jump to test muscular power in a basketball player provides comparable statistics to judge readiness for activities like jump shots and slam dunks.

Game-specific skill tests assess fitness to return by putting athletes through sport-specific drills (running, pivoting, passing, throwing). Athletes should be assessed by qualified staff to confirm they can complete game-related skills to an acceptable competitive level.

bandDescriptors.full: 6–8/8 — Explains how both skill tests AND physical tests indicate readiness. Covers pain-free full range of motion, strength comparison between injured and uninjured limb (90–95% benchmark), mobility/agility tests (e.g. Illinois Agility Test, circumduction test), and game-specific skill tests. Uses sport-specific examples. Explains why each test type matters for safe return.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–5/8 — Covers both skill and physical tests but with limited depth. Examples are generic or one type of test is explained in detail while the other is superficial. The 90–95% strength benchmark or injured/uninjured comparison may be missing.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/8 — Vague description of 'doing tests before returning' without distinguishing skill from physical tests or providing meaningful detail about what the tests involve.

writtenQuestions.q: Discuss the ethical issues to consider before an athlete returns to play following an injury. (5 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Two major ethical issues are the use of painkillers and pressure to participate.

Painkilling injections mask pain — the body's warning signal — so the athlete cannot feel further damage occurring. This desensitises the injured tissue, setting up an environment for additional rupturing and potentially permanent injury. Even oral painkillers like paracetamol mask symptoms that indicate healing is incomplete.

Pressure to return early can come from coaches, parents, contracts or fear of losing a position on the team. In children and young athletes, inexperienced coaches or parents can cause additional damage by pushing athletes to play before full recovery. This pressure breaches duty of care.

Policies requiring final medical clearance from a qualified doctor help prevent these ethical breaches by removing the decision from non-medical parties.

bandDescriptors.full: 5/5 — Identifies and explains BOTH major ethical issues: (1) painkiller use — masks pain signals, desensitises injured tissue, sets up further damage and permanent injury risk; AND (2) pressure to return — from coaches, contracts, or fear of losing team position. Mentions that final medical clearance from a qualified doctor removes the decision from non-medical parties.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/5 — Discusses both issues but the explanation of one is incomplete. May mention painkillers or pressure without fully explaining the mechanism by which each causes harm.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/5 — Identifies one ethical issue only, or lists both without any substantive explanation of why they are harmful.

writtenQuestions.q: Evaluate policies and procedures that address the ethical considerations in determining when an athlete returns to play from injury. (12 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Return-to-play policies in Australian sport directly address ethical concerns including pressure to participate and misuse of painkillers.

The NRL requires an 11-day mandatory stand-down; Netball Australia requires 14 days completely symptom-free before contact training plus a minimum 21-day overall stand-down; Boxing imposes a 30–90 day automatic suspension after a knockout with specialist neurological review. All three protocols mandate final medical clearance from a qualified doctor.

These policies prevent premature return driven by financial contracts, fear of losing team position, or parental and coach pressure. Painkilling injections are especially dangerous because they mask the body's warning signal, allowing further tissue damage and potentially permanent injury without the athlete's awareness.

By placing the decision solely with medical professionals, these policies uphold duty of care and remove pressure from coaches, managers and athletes themselves. However, not all sports have such policies, creating inequity in athlete protection.

Overall, these policies are effective in minimising ethical breaches and ensuring athletes return to sustained movement and performance safely (HM-12-09 / HM-12-10).

bandDescriptors.full: 9–12/12 — Names at least two specific policies with accurate detail (NRL 11-day stand-down, Netball Australia 14 days symptom-free + 21-day minimum, Boxing 30–90-day suspension + neurological review). Links each policy to the ethical issue it addresses — painkillers masking pain signals and pressure from coaches, contracts or fear of losing position. Makes a reasoned evaluative judgment on whether these policies effectively protect athlete welfare.
bandDescriptors.partial: 5–8/12 — Identifies policies with some correct detail but evaluation is limited to description rather than critical judgment. Ethical issues addressed but analysis lacks depth. More descriptive than evaluative.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–4/12 — Vague reference to return-to-play policies without naming specific sports or stand-down periods. Mentions ethical issues superficially. No evaluative judgment.

writtenQuestions.q: Outline the graduated return-to-play (GRTP) protocol for a junior netball player following a concussion. (6 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
Netball Australia's GRTP requires the player to be completely symptom-free for 14 days before beginning any graduated activity. The overall minimum return period for community-level players is 21 days.

The graduated steps are: (1) Complete rest until symptom-free → (2) Light aerobic exercise (walking, swimming) → (3) Sport-specific exercise (running drills, no contact) → (4) Non-contact training drills → (5) Medical clearance from a qualified doctor → (6) Return to full contact competition.

If symptoms return at any stage, the player must immediately return to the previous step and remain there until symptom-free. Final medical clearance is mandatory before full return to play.

bandDescriptors.full: 5–6/6 — States Netball Australia requires 14 days completely symptom-free before beginning graduated activity, with a minimum 21-day overall return period. Lists graduated steps in correct sequence. States that symptoms returning means stepping back, and that final medical clearance is mandatory before return.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/6 — Describes the graduated steps with some accuracy but omits or confuses the 14/21-day timing, misses the 'step back if symptoms return' rule, or omits mandatory medical clearance.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/6 — Describes a general graduated return process without Netball-specific details or timelines. May only say 'rest and gradually return to play'.

writtenQuestions.q: Compare the concussion return-to-play protocols for NRL, Netball and Boxing, explaining why the differences exist. (8 marks)
writtenQuestions.answer:
The three protocols differ significantly in their stand-down periods, reflecting the risk level of each sport.

The NRL requires an 11-day mandatory stand-down before any return to competition following a diagnosed concussion.

Netball Australia follows a more conservative approach: 14 days completely symptom-free before full contact training, with an overall minimum of 21 days for community-level players.

Boxing has the strictest protocol: after a knockout, the boxer faces an automatic 30–90 day suspension (longer for repeated KOs), plus mandatory specialist neurological review before clearance.

All three protocols require final medical clearance from a qualified doctor. The differences in stand-down periods reflect the varying levels of head trauma risk. Boxing's extended suspension acknowledges the direct targeting of the head and the high risk of cumulative brain damage from repeated knockouts. The NRL's shorter period reflects that concussions occur incidentally rather than by design, though the sport is still high contact.

bandDescriptors.full: 6–8/8 — Accurately states all three protocols: NRL (11-day), Netball Australia (14 days symptom-free + 21-day minimum), Boxing (30–90-day suspension + specialist neurological review). Notes all require final medical clearance. Explains WHY the differences exist — links stand-down length to head trauma risk level in each sport; notes Boxing targets the head directly and carries the highest cumulative brain damage risk.
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–5/8 — States most protocols with some correct numbers but one or two details are missing or slightly wrong. Explains differences exist due to varying risk levels but without specific reasoning per sport.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/8 — Names some sports without accurate stand-down details. Comparison is vague — 'some sports have longer rest periods' without specific figures or explanation of why.
